systems: Terraform (`plan -detailed-exitcode`: the changes-present exit is opt-in — the shape removed here)
git (`diff --exit-code` / `--quiet`: same opt-in shape; scripts must remember the flag)
Ansible (`--check --diff` exits non-zero on failure only; `changed` never reaches the exit code)
Kubernetes (`kubectl diff` exits 1 when differences are found, with no flag — the one surveyed default that already matches)
crux.verdict: accept(three of four surveyed tools carry the fail-open default forjar had, and it is the industry norm rather than a forjar invention: a diff verb that exits 0 over a diff unless asked. kubectl diff is the counterexample and the shape adopted. forjar's case is stronger than any of theirs because `drift` has one job and one consumer — a cron line or a CI step reads the code and never the text — so a verdict that stays on stdout is a verdict nobody reads. Where forjar is WEAKER than Terraform after this change: exit 1 is shared with a general error, where -detailed-exitcode distinguishes 2 (changes) from 1 (error); the book points a script that needs the distinction at --json's drift_count.)
